html:
The map's label for the Maya world of the Preclassic period, shown from 323 BCE to 400 CE: chiefdoms and early kingdoms across the Yucatán peninsula, Guatemala, Belize and Chiapas.

Maya farming villages spread through the lowlands from about 1000 BCE. Between 1000 and 400 BCE they began to build ceremonial centres with platforms and plazas, as at Nakbe. In the Late Preclassic, from about 400 BCE to 250 CE, came huge cities. El Mirador in northern Guatemala had pyramids among the largest ever built, and raised causeways linked it to its neighbours.

  • Kings: the San Bartolo murals, painted about 100 BCE, show the maize god and a king being crowned, so kingship was already in place.
  • Writing: the Maya script was in use by about 300 BCE.
  • Neighbours: the Maya took ideas from the Olmec and other Mesoamerican peoples, and highland cities such as Kaminaljuyu traded jade and obsidian.

Around 100 to 200 CE many great Preclassic centres, El Mirador among them, were abandoned, for reasons still debated. Then the Classic period began, with cities such as Tikal and Calakmul and powerful outside contacts, as when Teotihuacan intervened at Tikal in 378. The chart follows the whole story in the bar for the Maya city-states.
